summary:
Arcadia Planitia - Measured Terrain Planner is a terrain analysis and mission-planning tool designed to evaluate landing sites and navigation routes across Mars’s Arcadia Planitia region. By combining elevation datasets, slope modeling, and surface hazard mapping, the planner identifies safe, resource-accessible zones for autonomous rovers and future human habitats.
This project directly addresses the challenge of navigating uncharted planetary surfaces where steep gradients, boulders, and loose regolith pose major risks to mission hardware. Users can measure distances, inspect terrain profiles, and generate optimized waypoints in real time.
Arcadia Planitia is a prime candidate for future Mars exploration due to its flat topography and potential shallow subsurface water ice. Providing a reliable, data-driven way to assess this region helps mission planners reduce landing hazards, streamline surface operations, and support sustainable long-term exploration.
details:
The Explorers: Martian Map is designed to help astronauts plan surface exploration after landing on Mars. It brings terrain, imagery, environmental context, and scientific objectives into one interactive application, helping crews understand their surroundings and plan Marswalks between a habitat, landing site, and exploration destinations.

Users select a starting point and destination by entering coordinates, choosing suggested locations, or placing pins on the map. After pressing Get directions, the application compares the shortest route with an alternative that minimizes the maximum terrain slope. Routes respect the selected slope limit and available elevation coverage. Astronauts can inspect the landscape through layered 2D maps and interactive 3D terrain, then arrange science stops, specify observation times, set travel limits, and save or export a mission briefing.

The application integrates HiRISE optical imagery and elevation data, MOLA/HRSC regional elevation, THEMIS nighttime infrared imagery, supplied AR optical and geology records, and archived Mars Climate Database atmospheric samples. It supports exploration of Arcadia Planitia and Jezero Crater while clearly identifying dataset boundaries, missing measurements, and differences in resolution.

The intended benefit is to help future astronauts balance efficient travel, terrain difficulty, and scientific value. Combining these datasets in one workspace reduces the need to interpret disconnected maps and makes the relationship between terrain conditions and mission objectives easier to understand. Our current prototype also supports education and discussion about the challenges of human exploration on Mars.

We developed the interface using JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS. Leaflet powers the 2D map, while Three.js and WebGL render a terrain mesh derived from measured elevation. Web Workers handle route calculations and mesh preparation without blocking map interactions. The backend uses a TypeScript API running in a local Cloudflare Workers environment, with SQLite through D1 for saved plans. A Node.js HTTPS gateway encrypts communication, and Python supports data preparation and verification. The prototype runs on a standard computer with a modern WebGL-capable browser and can be accessed by other computers on the same Wi-Fi network.

Our creative contribution is connecting a familiar directions interface with planetary science evidence, 3D terrain inspection, and science itinerary planning. Rather than showing only a path, the application helps users examine why a route may be preferable and what scientific activities could be completed along it.

Our team considered astronaut mobility, terrain slopes, scientific priorities, interface responsiveness, accessibility, geographic accuracy, and uncertainty. Dark and light themes, keyboard controls, source information, and clear coverage messages support usability and transparency.

The current application is a research prototype requiring further validation before astronaut operations. Its lower-slope route does not assess every hazard, and archived atmospheric samples are not live weather. Oxygen consumption, spacesuit performance, and live radiation are not modeled. OpenAI Codex assisted with coding, integration, debugging, documentation, and testing; the scientific measurements and elevation-derived terrain were not generated by an AI model.
